---
title: "Poisson spike-train deconvolution"
description: "Recover overlapping peaks from noisy signals, including multichannel GC/MS data."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

In deconvolution, a design matrix contains shifted copies of the peak-shape
function, also called the point spread function. Sparse coefficients represent
sharp events, while the measured signal is blurred and noisy. For nonnegative
Poisson intensities,

\[
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}\{(X\beta)_i\},\qquad\beta\geq0.
\]

The following examples each have **10,000 observations, 10,000 candidate peak
locations and 1,000 true peaks**. L0glm fits the Poisson likelihood directly;
the native OpenMP backend shares the sparse convolution design across channels.
L0glm uses the GIC preset. Competing LASSO methods use ten lambda values,
selected by GIC or native five-fold CV with weighted prediction error.
See [benchmark hardware and timing conventions](performance.html#reproduce-and-extend).

## Single channel deconvolution

```{r single, eval=FALSE}
library(L0glm)
single <- simul(method=2L, n=10000L, p=10000L,
  n_nonzero=1000L, seed=2L)
system.time(fit <- L0glm.fit(single$X, single$y, family=poisson("identity"),
  lambda="gic", nonnegative=TRUE, intercept=FALSE, relaxed=TRUE,
  parallelize=TRUE, ncores=4L))
L0glm.metrics(fit, beta_true=single$beta_true)[c("gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN",
  "F1_score", "MCC")]
```

<!-- BEGIN single-speed -->
L0glm recovers **845 of 1,000 true peaks with just 154 false positives** in **0.20 seconds**: **2× faster than GIC-tuned LASSO** and **34× faster than relaxed LASSO tuned by five-fold CV** in this comparison.
<!-- END single-speed -->

The table compares the GIC-preset fit with LASSO and fully relaxed LASSO,
each selected by GIC or five-fold CV over the same ten-value lambda grid.
The GIC comparison is available through `sparseglm()`:

```{r single-comparison, eval=FALSE}
gic <- sparseglm(single, family=poisson("identity"),
  method=c("lasso", "relaxed_lasso"), tune="gic", nlambda=10L,
  nonnegative=TRUE, intercept=FALSE, approximation="wls")
```

## Multichannel deconvolution

**Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC/MS)** provides a natural application:
compounds with overlapping chromatographic peaks contribute counts across many
mass-to-charge channels. Peak locations are shared across channels, while each
compound has its own sparse mass spectrum. A grouped Poisson model recovers the
peak locations and the corresponding spectra together.

The simulation retains **all 226 informative mass channels** generated from the
spectral library. No channels are discarded for fitting or plotting.

```{r multi, eval=FALSE}
multi <- simul(method=4L, n=10000L, p=10000L,
  n_nonzero=1000L, seed=2L)
system.time(fit_multi <- L0glm.fit(multi$X, multi$y, family=poisson("identity"),
  lambda="gic", nonnegative=TRUE, intercept=FALSE, grouped=TRUE, relaxed=TRUE,
  parallelize=TRUE, ncores=4L))
L0glm.metrics(fit_multi, beta_true=multi$beta_true)[c("gic", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN",
  "F1_score", "MCC", "within_row_F1_score", "within_row_MCC")]
```

<!-- BEGIN multi-speed -->
L0glm recovers **944 of 1,000 true peaks with just 11 false positives** in **9.63 seconds**: **25× faster than GIC-tuned group LASSO** and **332× faster than relaxed group LASSO tuned by five-fold CV** in this comparison.
<!-- END multi-speed -->

<!-- BEGIN multi-metrics -->
| Method | Selection | Seconds | GIC | TP | FP | FN | TN | F1 | MCC | Within-row F1 | Within-row MCC |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| L0glm | GIC preset | 9.63 | 5615963 | 944 | 11 | 56 | 8989 | 0.966 | 0.962 | 0.909 | 0.864 |
| Group LASSO | GIC path | 244.87 | 7413616 | 980 | 860 | 20 | 8140 | 0.690 | 0.685 | 0.842 | 0.768 |
| Relaxed group LASSO | GIC path | 906.34 | 6138687 | 909 | 309 | 91 | 8691 | 0.820 | 0.802 | 0.853 | 0.782 |
| Group LASSO | 5-fold CV | 813.42 | 9639345 | 998 | 4242 | 2 | 4758 | 0.320 | 0.316 | 0.886 | 0.830 |
| Relaxed group LASSO | 5-fold CV | 3199.62 | 6198648 | 962 | 502 | 38 | 8498 | 0.781 | 0.769 | 0.856 | 0.785 |
<!-- END multi-metrics -->

Row F1 and MCC measure recovery of peak times. Within-row F1 and MCC measure
mass-spectrum sparsity among correctly recovered true-positive peaks.
Group LASSO and relaxed group LASSO use glmnet's grouped Gaussian approximation, with shared
row weights `1/(rowMeans(y)+0.1)`; every selected model is evaluated using the
original Poisson likelihood and the same GIC. Each glmnet path has ten lambda
values. Relaxed group LASSO refits the selected shared row support with `gamma=0`.
Native `cv.glmnet()` selects the minimum weighted prediction error using five
common random folds and four parallel workers. L0glm uses a single GIC preset
with four outcome-fitting threads. CV timings include worker startup and
the full-data refit; simulation and final metric reporting are excluded.
The L0glm time is the median of three fits with matching coefficients.

```{r multi-comparison, eval=FALSE}
gic_multi <- sparseglm(multi, family=poisson("identity"),
  method=c("lasso", "relaxed_lasso"), tune="gic", nlambda=10L,
  nonnegative=TRUE, intercept=FALSE, approximation="wls_grouped")
```

The [benchmark source](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/benchmark_website_deconvolution.R)
reproduces both selection rules, the timings and every reported metric.

### Correlated peaks and group LASSO

Shifted copies of the point-spread function are strongly correlated. For this
design, the standard group-LASSO irrepresentability diagnostic is **20.54**,
well above the bound of one. This helps explain why group LASSO can retain many
neighbouring peak locations even while reconstructing the observed signal well.
L0glm's direct support penalty gives a much cleaner separation of the peaks.

To compute the diagnostic, let \(A\) be the shared-row-weighted design with
columns scaled to unit norm, \(S\) the true row support and
\(U_{j\cdot}=B^*_{j\cdot}/\|B^*_{j\cdot}\|_2\). We evaluate

\[
\max_{j\notin S}\left\|
A_j^\top A_S(A_S^\top A_S)^{-1}U_S
\right\|_2.
\]

The standard group-LASSO selection conditions require this quantity to be at
most one, with a strict inequality giving a sufficient condition under the
assumptions in [Bach (2008)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v9/bach08b.html).
This diagnostic concerns the unconstrained weighted-Gaussian group model;
the benchmark additionally uses nonnegativity constraints and Poisson scoring.
The [diagnostic script](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/check_group_irrepresentability.R)
gives the calculation and numerical solve check.

## Tune or use native validation

```{r tune, eval=FALSE}
gic <- L0glm.tune(multi$X, multi$y, family=poisson("identity"),
  tune="gic", nlambda=10L, nonnegative=TRUE, grouped=TRUE, relaxed=TRUE)
cv <- L0glm.tune(multi$X, multi$y, family=poisson("identity"),
  tune="cv", nfolds=5L, nlambda=10L, nonnegative=TRUE, grouped=TRUE, relaxed=TRUE)
```

For held-out checkpoint stopping, supply `validation=list(X=V, y=v)`.
OpenMP remains available through the native backend. See the
[validation example](controls.html#held-out-early-stopping) and the full
[benchmark tables](performance.html).

The L0 deconvolution idea was inspired by work by
[de Rooi & Eilers (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aca.2011.05.030).
Our methods for automatically setting regularization, the extensions to Poisson
or negative-binomial noise, and the multichannel shared-support extensions are
new developments of the present work. `simul()` supports all three noise models.
